FASCISM'S SPREAD.

It is the natural boast of the rulers and founders of what is known as Fascism, that it has spread abroad and that the movement is to be found in forty countries including Conservative England. On the 23rd of March last, the Fascisti celebrated the sixth anniversary of the foundation of their party. It was first known as Fascio di Combattimento and at the inaugural meeting presided over by the now recognised high priest of the craft—Benito Mussolini—held in a small back room in Milan, there were present 200 adherents. In 1921 the Fascio di Combattimento became the Fascist Party of Italy, and thirty Fascist members were returned to Parliament. Like most movements that have come to birth and remained active, the original ideas or rules which governed the organisation are little heard of today. The 1919 programme contained such things as the abolition of the Senate, the introduction of woman suffrage, partial workers' control in industry, a heavy progressive tax on capital, sequestration of religions properties, nationalisation of all factories for arms and explosives, and other aims that might readily be described as purely Sociistic.

Whatever may be said against the movement, the fact that it has existed so long is not to be despised, whilst the fact also that it has made Italy a country to be reckoned with, has also to be noted. Outside Italy the Fascist
movement is not likely to take any great hold on the minds of the people in the country in which it has found a temporary resting place.
Rubber Prospects.

The answer to the doubt expressed on the question of rubber restriction is best found in the present position of the rubber market. There is a growing demand—prices rule steady and have an upward tendency, whilst share values are inclined the same way. Had Dutch producers co-operated in the scheme of restriction there is no saying what present conditions would be. The Dutch have pursued a lone course, for reasons satisfactory to themselves. Restriction of output has helped to reduce the large stocks of rubber that were in storage when the slump set in and continued so disastrously until the situation was firmly handled. Planters, dealers, and holders of shares have all had what is known as a "thin" time. Singapore was likened to a City of the dead. But all this is becoming ancient history. Reports of Singapore companies—and of course rubber companies are not all stationed there—breathe hope for the future, and inspire confidence by reason of their ability to make forward sale contracts, and pay dividends.

The Continent is the cock-pit of Europe. They grow bitter weeds there, and the result is death and the thing that leads to death—war. As the number one Robot said—"Read History." Why certain parts of Europe should breed the pestilential trait of mind to be found in unholy and senseless anarchy no one seems to know. It may be that minds brood more deeply than in the colder clime of Britain where the motto might be said to be—"Be slow to anger." Why should there be a desire to "remove" Mr. Austen Chamberlain, the British Foreign Secretary? What object would be gained in taking away a life which it would be generally admitted, is and has been, stainless? There is no sensible answer to such a question. The present Government has seen fit to reverse its predecessor's arrangement with the Russian Soviet Government. It might be said that the electorate gave it a mandate to do so. It may be that certain elements in Russia see in this a just cause for "direct action." Such a line of thought is beyond understanding. That it exists on the Continent is obvious. That Governments are not able to guard against it has already been proved. All the more reason then why the persons of those who serve the nation so ably, conscientiously and well should be guarded with the utmost care; more especially when the exercise of their duties call them to "foreign parts."

Bible Facts.
(To the Editor of this China Mail).
Sir,—Will you kindly allow me for the second and last time a little space in your valuable paper?
I wish I could have enough of spare time to answer all the questions raised by your correspondents about the Bible; but unfortunately I cannot afford it at present.
I shall only try at present to show Nuda Veritas how ridiculous his letter as a whole is.
On the one hand he says he believes strongly in God, while on the other he totally ridicules the Bible. " How did he arrive at the belief of God then?

Again, he tries to say that he is all the time hinting at the modification of the Bible. Why, if the Bible were written by savages or barbarians, what can he expect to modify in it? It must be all rot, or nonsense...

The fact that the Bible was written in an age of barbarians simply adds to its authenticity, since it is impossible for any sensible person to imagine that barbarians are such able writers who can produce such a great textbook as the Bible to be used by millions of people for thousands of years, unless those barbarians, as our friend calls them, are inspired.
Hongkong, April 30.
Fire Insurance.
To the Editor of the China Mail.

Your correspondent also complained of the lack of action by the Government in that facilities for fighting fire are not at the disposal of all Peak residents. I would add that the Government are to blame even more for the state of affairs in places such as Sai On Lane where are godowns huddled together in a street which can be crossed in two or three paces and as the owners of these godowns are not called upon by law to fit them up with automatic sprinklers of course they won't go to the expense. If they only knew it they are having to pay out in heavier premiums quite as much as it would cost them to fit up such apparatus, and who can blame the Companies for wanting a heavy premium when there have been fires galore in that district?

The merchants won't move in the matter so it is up to the Government. We have not insurance inspectors here such as there are at the places your correspondent of yesterday mentioned but we certainly ought to have, and matters such as these would fall to their lot. One good result which would inevitably follow their observations would be the recommendation of the demolition of many buildings and their erection more in accordance with requirements. Something might even eventuate in the nature of town planning. Although it is rather late in the day to start that, the need of some reform however small is so obvious that it hits in the face anyone who is called upon to visit districts such as I mentioned in the earlier part of my letter. After all if Manila can do it why can't Hongkong?
Hongkong, April 30.
Fire Facts.
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—With regard to your editorial comments on the need for co-operation by the public in anti-fire measures by the installation of their own appliances I think a good many of us were at the demonstration held at Statue Square a few years ago.

I hold no brief for any of the agents of the extinguishers used on that occasion, neither had the police and Fire Brigade Department under whose auspices the display was arranged, but I can believe what I saw with my own eyes, and that was the putting out in seconds, barrels of blazing oil and other oil soaked inflammable material.

ONE WHO WAS THERE.
Hongkong, April 30
SHREDS AND PATCHFS.

May day festivals
MAY DAY, are not uncommon at Home. The festival itself has existed, though its form has often changed from the earliest times. It came to the English from the Druids, who themselves had it from India. The Druids celebrated the worship of the God Bel on the first of May, by lighting immense fires in honour of him upon the various carns, and hence the day is called by the aboriginal Irish and Scotch Highlanders, la Bealtine, Bealtaine or Beltime, that is, the day of Belen's fire. Going-a-Maying is an old custon. In the days of long ago the juveniles of both sexes were worn to rise a little after midnight and walk to some neighbouring wood, accompanied with music and blowing of horns, where they broke down branches from the trees, and adorned themselves with nosegays and crowns of flowers; when this was done they returned with their booty homewards about the rising of the sun, and made their doors and windows to triumph with their flowery spoils. Here is an interesting Penys diary note under May 1, 1667. "To Westminster; on the way meeting many milkmolds, with their garlands upon their pails, dancing with a fiddler before them, and saw pretty Nelly (Nell Gwynne) standing at her lodgings do r in Drury Lane in her smock sleeves and bodice, looking upon on"; she seemed a mighty pretty creature.

FRIDAY, an unlucky day, but, according to astrology, quite the reverse, especially to lovers. The day is named after Freiya, the Noise goddess of love and marriage, therefore the Scottish custom of making it the favourite day for weddings is correct.

TRAFFIC
FRIENDS.
Thanks either to an efficient traffic control or the humane and other feelings of the

users of motor vehicles, Hongkong is in no danger of traffic fends. The press certainly does not overflow with accounts of traffic offences. Should that unhappy time ever arrive two ways suggest themselves of meeting the problem. A recent talk with the head of the Manila police revealed how he and his merry men deal with offenders. First of all a courteous letter is sent pointing out the misdeed. Should the sin be repeated another, but firmer letter is sent. On the third occasion the law is set in motion and the offender brought to book. This is consideration unlimited, more so seeing the thousands of vehicles—including horse or pony drawn, which are to be seen in the Manila Streets. Incidenatly it may be added that the Chief of Police is strongly in favour of there being no hindrance to swift moving vehicles. There is less danger from speed than there is from slowness. Another method of dealing with road hogs is that adopted in at least one part of America. A, photograph discloses a policeman on his motor bike. He is noting something in a book. Instead of a sidecar there is a large cage, heavily padlocked. Inside the cage there is an infringer of the traffic laws being taken to Jall so that he "may serve as a reminder and warning to others." Some method!

Is the hiring out of cats to kill rats becoming a new industry? Abroad

It is a quite common thing for a certain number of cats to be on the strength of the municipal staff, and now London firms are employing cats at fixed salaries. One firm with warehouses near the river has just contracted for a large number of cats to be supplied, for which they are to pay 15s. 2d. per annum for each cat. This will include their food, for it is a mistake to think that cats can live entirely on rats and mice. "An unrelieved rodent" diet for cats is as bad as nothing but meat for a hunter," said an official of the R.S.P.C.A. In Hongkong, the absence of cats is very noticeable. Dogs predominate. It is a case of "love me, love my dog"; and very often they are more trouble than they are worth; scare unoffending people to death; bite them often, and scarcely if ever scare away thieves. There are classic examples of the dog who has been known to be quiet while its owner's possessions were being rifled.

HONGKONG'S
FAME.
Hongkong, it is well known often figures in books of travel.

But how often in novels? Two novels occur to the mind, written by well-known writers, where a great deal of the action takes place in Hongkong. Unfortunately both books deal with a phase of life not generally mentioned. in or at family prayers. Gilbert Frankau was the first "offender". It can be said of the book that its description of Hongkong places was generally accurate. A greater than Frankau has gone to Hongkong and his book has been the cause of some discussion and not a little speculation. We may leave it at that. Protest that Hongkong is not so bad as the place is painted would be in vain. And in dealing with books it is an unfortunate fact that the generality of reader condemns the subject matter of a book rather than the way that subject matter has been handled. It may be a dangerous doctrine to preach, but the suggestion arises that provided a writer is honest it matters not what he writes about.
Some one has been saying nice things about the saxophone.

SAXOPHONE about the saxophone, which will probably encourage Kowloon players. The saxophone was not an accident by any means, we are told having been invented by Antoine Joseph Sax, born at Dinant, Belgium, November 6, 1814, the son of a reed instrument maker. He studied at the Brussels Conservatoire of Music and his proficiency on both the flute and the clarinet became marked. There were many opportunities for Sax to become a musician of note, but he preferred to return to the bench. Moving to Paris in 1842, Sax produced the first "saxhorn" in 1843. In 1846 a soprano saxophone was manufactured and patented, followed by the alto, tenor and baritone saxophone. Since then some of us have desired to follow certain saxophone players, but have desisted when realising that others would only take the matter up!

It was from this shop that the tea which was thrown into Boston Harbour during the Boston Tea Party" in 1773 was exported. This incident was really the beginning of the American War of Independence. It is said that the number of horn-rimmed spectacles sign in Creschursh Lane this year is as a record. The tea shop is a frenzied pilgrimage for American visitors.
